Agad na inaksyunan ng mga kawani ng Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) at Caloocan Public Safety and Transport Management Department (PSTMD) ang pagputol sa mga nakausling sanga at mga nakakalat na dahon na umaabot sa bike lane sa Bonifacio Monument Circle.

Mahalagang alisin ang anumang sagabal na maaaring magdulot ng aksidente o panganib sa mga dumaraang bikers at iba pang road users. 

Ang mga nakausling sanga at kalat sa bike lane ay maaaring maging sanhi ng pag-iwas o pagdulas ng mga siklista. Bukod dito, maaari rin itong magdulot ng trapiko.

Patuloy ang koordinasyon at mabilis na pagtugon ng MMDA at pamahalaang lungsod upang mapanatiling ligtas at maayos ang mga kalsada para sa lahat.

data.text:
Want to know why the Gulf states will want the total eradication of the Iranian regime FAST?

Here’s why.

The entire economic survival of the Gulf runs through one narrow waterway: the Strait of Hormuz.

In 2025 alone:

• ~13 million barrels of oil per day passed through it
• ~31% of global seaborne crude
• 20–30% of globally traded petroleum liquids
• 20–25% of global LNG exports (mostly from Qatar)

Shut it down and the economic shock hits within days.

Here’s who gets hit the hardest.

Gulf exporters (their economies depend on exports leaving through Hormuz):

🚨 Iraq

~4–4.5M barrels/day exported through the strait

90%+ of government revenue tied to it

$300–400M lost per day

🚨 Kuwait

~2–2.5M barrels/day exported

~95% of shipments rely on Hormuz

Annual losses could exceed $70B

🚨 Qatar

Controls 20–25% of global LNG supply

LNG exports = 70–80% of its economy

$200–300M lost per day

🚨 United Arab Emirates

~2.5–3M barrels/day exports

~40–50% can bypass via pipeline

The rest gets stranded

🚨 Saudi Arabia

6–7M barrels/day exports

Can reroute ~5M via pipelines

Still faces 20–40% export disruption

Asian economies that depend on Hormuz energy:

About 84–89% of oil leaving the Gulf goes to Asia.

The biggest exposure:

🚩 China

~40–55% of oil imports pass through Hormuz

Losing it means a 4–6M barrels/day supply shock

🚩 India

60%+ of oil imports come through the Gulf

53% of LNG comes from Qatar/UAE

🚩 Japan

80%+ of energy imports transit Hormuz

🚩 South Korea

80%+ of energy imports rely on Hormuz

🚩 Pakistan

~99% of LNG imports come from Qatar/UAE

🚩 Bangladesh

~72% of LNG imports come through this route

🚩 Thailand & Philippines

Highly import dependent

Major exposure to oil price spikes

But here’s the part people miss.

The Gulf states don’t just export through Hormuz.

They survive off imports coming back through it.

Food, medicine, and consumer goods.

Food dependency:

Saudi Arabia – ~80% food imports

United Arab Emirates – ~90%

Qatar – ~95%

Kuwait – ~90%

Bahrain – ~85%

If the strait closes:

Oil could spike to $100–140 per barrel

LNG prices could triple

Shipping costs could jump 250%

Maritime traffic could drop ~70%

So the survival clock looks roughly like this:

• Export revenue collapse: immediately
• Global energy supply shock: within days
• Fuel price spikes across Asia: within days
• Food & goods shortages in Gulf states: 2–4 weeks
• Severe economic instability: 1–2 months

Now connect the dots.

As long as the regime in Iran can threaten the Strait of Hormuz, the entire Gulf economic system sits under a loaded gun.

That’s why if conflict escalates, the Gulf states won’t want a drawn-out war.

They’ll want it ended fast.

So now you should understand why this military action is going as fast as possible.

The Regime will collapse in less than a week.

WTA Indian Wells 

Donna Vekic vs Tereza Valentova

🧠 Form & Context

🇭🇷 Donna Vekic (#100, right-handed; 179 cm)
📉 2026: 5–6 overall | 5–6 on hard
✅ Recent: Manila F (L vs Osorio); Merida 1R (L vs Bucsa)
🔁 Indian Wells track record: R16 in 2025 (has handled these conditions before)
⚠️ Hard-52 red flags: MS Hold% 54.7, DF% 9.1, 2nd-serve win% 36.4, DR 0.90 → fragile profile on slow hard

🇨🇿 Tereza Valentova (#46, right-handed; —)
📈 2026: 8–5 overall | 8–5 on hard
✅ Recent: AO 3R (L vs Rybakina); Doha 2R (L vs Muchova)
🚀 Momentum + ceiling: heavy early-season tour exposure, plus strong lower-level winning base
⚠️ Note: Dubai retirement listed (monitor physically), but underlying hard indicators still strong: DR 1.09, Hold% 64.3, Break% 42.5

🔍 Match Breakdown
Indian Wells’ slow hard / high-bounce environment tends to stretch points and punish shaky second serves—and that’s where this matchup tilts.

Valentova’s path to control: attack Vekic’s second-serve vulnerability and keep returns deep to force Vekic into extra balls. With Vekic’s Hold%/2nd-serve numbers in the danger zone, sustained pressure should create multiple break looks per set.

Vekic’s path to flip it: she needs a high first-serve percentage and fast, first-strike patterns (serve +1, early forehand drives) to avoid getting dragged into high-bounce rallies. Her experience and past IW runs matter most if she can keep sets “serve-dominant.”

Swing factor: Valentova’s listed Dubai retirement is the only real “brake.” If movement/endurance is compromised, Vekic can steal momentum by shortening points and leaning into veteran shot selection.

🔮 Prediction
Valentova has the cleaner, more stable profile for this specific Indian Wells test: better balance in hold/break dynamics and a return-led pattern that targets Vekic’s biggest structural issue (second serve + DFs). Vekic’s route is narrow but real—she’s experienced here and can still spike level if the first serve lands and she dictates early.

🧩 Prediction: Valentova
